title: Earth's Building Blocks Came From Its Own Neighborhood, Study Finds
summary:
For decades, planetary scientists have debated where Earth's raw material came from. Many thought 6 to 40 percent of it drifted in from the outer Solar System, beyond Jupiter. That idea helped explain how Earth got water and other volatile substances — materials that turn to gas easily.

New research challenges that picture. Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower of ETH Zurich compared isotope measurements from a wide range of meteorites with Earth's own composition. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses — like siblings who weigh slightly different amounts.

The team used ten isotope systems. Earlier studies usually relied on just two. "Our studies are actually data science experiments," Sossi said. They ran statistical calculations rarely used in geochemistry.

The conclusion: Earth formed entirely from inner Solar System material. Outer material makes up less than 2 percent of Earth's mass — possibly none at all. The study appeared in Nature Astronomy.

"We were truly astonished to find that the Earth is composed entirely of material from the inner Solar System," Bower said.

Scientists divide meteorites into two groups. Non-carbonaceous meteorites formed in the inner Solar System. Carbonaceous ones, richer in water and carbon, came from the outer region. Earth, the analysis says, is made only of the inner kind.

Why two separate reservoirs? Jupiter likely played a role. As the gas giant grew, its gravity carved a gap in the disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Jupiter acted like a barrier, limiting how much outer material could move inward. Until now, scientists didn't know how effective that barrier was.

The finding suggests Earth grew in a relatively stable environment, gathering nearby planetary bodies. It also means water and other volatiles were probably present in the inner Solar System from the start — no delivery from far away needed.
why_it_matters: This rewrites the origin story of our own planet: if Earth's water and carbon were local rather than shipped in from the outer Solar System, then rocky planets around other stars might start out with the ingredients for life far more often than scientists assumed.

background_read: ETH Zurich (the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich) is one of Europe's leading research universities, and Nature Astronomy is a peer-reviewed journal that publishes space and planetary science.
For decades, the leading explanation for Earth's water was delivery from afar: icy bodies from beyond Jupiter — carbonaceous meteorites and comets — crashing into the young planet.

Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System, and its gravity is stronger than any other planet's. Planetary scientists have long argued that as Jupiter grew, it opened a gap in the swirling disc of gas and dust (the protoplanetary disc) that surrounded the newborn Sun; one well-known version of this idea, the 'Grand Tack', pictures Jupiter wandering inward and then back out, reshaping the early Solar System.

Meteorites act as free samples of that early era. The carbon-rich, water-rich kind (carbonaceous chondrites) formed farther out, while the drier, non-carbonaceous kind formed closer in, and their chemistry works like a fingerprint.
Isotopes are the tool for reading those fingerprints, because the same element can come in slightly heavier or slightly lighter versions — exactly what Sossi and Bower measured.

perspectives.perspective: Supportive — planetary scientists who favour a local origin
perspectives.description: The team's ten isotope systems point to a single source for Earth, and the mix of meteorite chemistry and statistics gives the 'everything came from nearby' camp its strongest evidence yet. It also makes Earth less of a lucky exception.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — researchers who backed outer-Solar-System delivery
perspectives.description: Models that brought in water aboard comets and carbon-rich meteorites lose their main explanation for Earth's oceans. Some will also question whether heavy statistical methods and a limited set of meteorites can really settle such a huge question, so the debate may not be over.

This is a classic scientific upgrade: replacing two-isotope comparisons with a broad statistical fingerprint. It also puts a number on a long-hypothesised mechanism — Jupiter acting as a gatekeeper in the young Solar System.
The next steps are checking whether inner-Solar-System material really can hold that much water, testing more meteorites and samples, and applying the same logic to other planetary systems.
